QUESTION OF THE WEEK - Economists were asked for their preliminary forecasts of third quarter GDP(A). These forecasts may change markedly between now and the release of the GDP data on December 4, but they do give a guide as to what sort of growth economists are looking at for the quarter. Positive growth is expected, above the June quarter rise of 0.1 percent but well below the March quarter's 2.0 percent rise.

Because the strong 2.0 percent rise of the September 1995 quarter drops out of annual calculations, the year to growth rate will decline markedly to around three percent, from 4.5 percent in the June quarter, assuming no revisions to previous data.

While some said the 2.4 percent retail trade rise in July suggested a good start for the quarter, others said the fact it was driven by clearance sales suggested stock rundown could be a detraction from growth. The strong 1.5 percent forecast was based on an expected strong rural contribution.

DWELLING UNIT COMMENCEMENTS - Most are looking for a small fall in line with the pretty flat level of approvals in the months up to May. Economists said June building approvals would affect June quarter starts because of the delay between approval and commencement. After the March quarter figure was inflated by projects approved up to a year earlier but held off until that quarter, some are looking for bit of corrective weakness this quarter.

LABOUR FORCE - Employment may receive a boost of between 10,000 and 15,000 from the hiring of Census collectors in August, and so economists said a strongish headline figure should be treated with some caution. If employment rises in line with the median forecast, it will be the fifth straight month of positive jobs growth, but employment will still only be about 20,000 higher than it was at the end of last year.

Generally, economists expect jobs growth will only be enough to match new entrants to the labour market, keeping the unemployment rate around 8.5 percent, and as long as it does it will fuel speculation of a fourth quarter rate cut. This should ensure that this data remains one of the most watched monthly releases until the end of this year. Real strength in employment growth is not expected until well into 1997, reflecting the lag of employment behind the rest of the economy, economists said.
